```{=html}
<ol>
<li>A histogram counts hours per bin: with 1-point bins, 74% of the 2,716 hours lie from −2% up to +3%; the errors run from −8.3% to +9.8%.</li>
<li>Center: mean +0.8%, median +0.7%. Demand came in above the forecast in 61% of hours.</li>
<li>Spread: standard deviation 2.45 points; mean ± 1 SD, from −1.65% to +3.25%, holds 72% of hours; the quartiles are −0.8% and +2.2%.</li>
<li>Chance by counting: 134 of 2,716 hours, 4.9%, had demand more than 5% above the forecast.</li>
<li>Nominal intervals from percentiles: 50% from −0.8% to +2.2%; 80% from −2.1% to +3.8% (lesson 4's band); 95% from −3.5% to +6.2%. Hours tied at the ends make them hold 51.3%, 81.1% and 95.0%.</li>
<li>Samples scatter: the standard error of that share is 6.8 points for 10 random hours, 2.2 for 100 and 0.7 for 1,000.</li>
<li>Independence (illustrative): gas plants A and B, each out in 5% of hours, are both out in 0.25% of hours, about 22 a year, only if their outages are independent.</li>
<li>Expected value: with plants A (150 MW) and B (100 MW) each out 5% of the time, 12.5 MW are out on average.</li>
</ol>
```

## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="k5-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Histogram</dt><dd>Hours counted per bin of error; the bin width changes how jagged it looks, not the data.</dd>
<dt>Mean and median</dt><dd>Two centers: the average, pulled by every value, and the middle value, which a few wild values barely move.</dd>
<dt>Standard deviation, quartiles</dt><dd>Two spreads: a typical distance from the mean, and the range of the middle half.</dd>
<dt>Percentile and interval</dt><dd>The value a given share of hours stays at or below; two of them bound an interval.</dd>
<dt>Probability as a share</dt><dd>Count the hours where the event happened and divide by all hours; with few hours, the share is rough.</dd>
<dt>Independence</dt><dd>When one event says nothing about the other, the chance of both is the product; a shared cause breaks it.</dd>
<dt>Expected value</dt><dd>Each outcome times its chance, added up; expected values add with or without independence.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>The formulas, and how sure a sample is</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Mean.** $\bar e = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i$, where $e_i$ is hour $i$'s error in % and $n = 2716$ hours.
- **Standard deviation.** $s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (e_i - \bar e)^2}$, in percentage points. Dividing by $n - 1$, as many tools do, gives 2.4533 points against 2.4528: with this many hours the choice hardly matters.
- **Percentile.** Sort the errors and write the share as a fraction $p$ ($p = 0.9$ for the 90th percentile). The percentile sits at position $(n - 1)\,p$ counting from 0, between two neighbours when that is not a whole number.
- **How sure a share is.** All 2,716 hours have the share $p = 134/2716$, 4.9%, above +5%. Across repeated random samples of $m$ hours, the sample share scatters around $p$ by about $\sqrt{p\,(1 - p)/m}$, its [standard error]{.lx-term term="standard-error"}; times 100, it is in percentage points.
- **The scatter by sample size.** 6.8 points for $m$ = 10 hours, 2.2 for 100 and 0.7 for 1,000.
- **Two standard errors.** For large samples, about 95% of estimates land within two standard errors. A sample of 100 hours with 9% above: 4.9% + 2 × 2.2 ≈ 9.3%, so 9% is within two standard errors.
- **Small samples.** With 10 hours the rule is rough: the share can only be 0%, 10%, 20% and so on.
- **Draws with replacement.** Each draw can pick any hour, even one already drawn, so the draws are independent with the same chances. Real hours in a row may move together, which this sampling leaves out.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Distributions as model inputs (a preview)</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Where these ideas go next.** Running a model on many random draws of its inputs: Modeler lesson [M7](m07-monte-carlo.html). Planning against scenarios weighted by their chances: [M8](m08-stochastic-robust.html). Fast stand-ins for slow models, each prediction with its own spread: [M9](m09-surrogates-uq.html).
- **Draw together what moves together.** Sample whole hours or days, so demand, wind and outages keep their joint behavior; drawing each input separately assumes independence.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="k5-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="interval" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Next winter, 95% of hours will fall inside this page's 95% interval.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It holds 95% of the 2,716 hours it was built from, by construction. Other months are untested, and from May the two reported series disagree.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="product" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Two plants that are each out in 5% of hours are both out in 0.25% of hours.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth, as a general rule. The product holds only if the outages are independent; a shared cause makes both-out hours more common.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="wild" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Adding one +100% reading to these 2,716 hours moves the median less than the mean.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. Adding one +100% reading to these hours moves the mean by +0.04 points and the median by 0.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="k5">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="centre" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">Five hourly errors: −1%, 0%, +1%, +2%, +8%. Their mean and median?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Mean +2%, median +1%</li><li data-value="b">Mean +1%, median +2%</li><li data-value="c">Both +2%</li><li data-value="d">Mean +2%, median 0%</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Mean +2% (the sum, +10%, over 5); median +1%, the middle of the sorted five. The +8% pulls the mean up, not the median.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="sample" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A random sample of 100 of these hours has 9% above +5%; all 2,716 hours have 4.9%. The best reading?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">The forecast got worse</li><li data-value="b">A share from 100 hours is rough; 9% is within its usual scatter</li><li data-value="c">9% is the true chance</li><li data-value="d">Samples cannot tell you anything</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Rough. Step 6 showed shares from 100 hours scattering by several points from sample to sample, so one sample at 9% is no sign the forecast changed. Go deeper · Analyst puts a number on that scatter.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<tbody>
<tr><td class="n">+0.8% and +0.7%</td><td>Mean and median error: demand above the day-ahead forecast in 61% of hours.</td><td class="s">Our calculation from <a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/">EIA-930</a> · SPP, Jan–Apr 2025</td></tr>
<tr><td class="n">2.45 points</td><td>Standard deviation of the errors.</td><td class="s">Same data</td></tr>
<tr><td class="n">−2.1% to +3.8%</td><td>The nominal middle 80% of the hours: lesson 4's band.</td><td class="s">Same data</td></tr>
<tr><td class="n">4.9%</td><td>Share of hours with demand more than 5% above the forecast (134 hours).</td><td class="s">Same data</td></tr>
<tr><td class="n">p × q</td><td>The chance two events both happen, where p and q are their separate chances: only if they are independent.</td><td class="s">Definition</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>
```
